subject: ela
skillName: Ask and answer about a speaker
intro: When someone is speaking — a classmate, teacher, or visitor — a good listener pays attention and then asks questions. You might ask because something was unclear, because you want to learn more, or because you want to check your understanding. You should also be able to answer questions about what a speaker said. The key is that your questions and answers should be connected to what the speaker actually said.

items.prompt: A classmate says: 'My uncle works on a fishing boat. They go out really early in the morning and catch fish all day.' A student wants to learn more. What is a good question to ask?

steps: The classmate shared information about her uncle's job on a fishing boat.
A good question gathers more information or clarifies something.
Example good question: 'How early do they go out on the boat?' or 'What kind of fish do they catch?'
These questions are connected to what the speaker said and ask for more detail.
solution.answer: 'What kind of fish does your uncle catch?' or 'How early in the morning do they leave?' — both gather more information about the speaker's topic.

items.prompt: A student gives a short speech: 'My favorite season is winter because I love playing in the snow and drinking hot cocoa.' A listener did not understand what hot cocoa is. What question should the listener ask?

steps: The listener is confused about a specific word or idea the speaker used.
A good clarifying question asks directly about the unclear part.
Good question: 'What is hot cocoa?' or 'What does hot cocoa taste like?'
solution.answer: 'What is hot cocoa?' — this clarifies something the listener did not understand from the speaker's statement.

items.prompt:
A teacher finishes explaining a science lesson. A student says, 'I want to ask a question.' He asks: 'What is your favorite color?' Is this a good question about the speaker's topic?
A) Yes
B) No — it is not connected to what the speaker said.

steps: Questions about a speaker should be about what the speaker said.
'What is your favorite color?' has nothing to do with the science lesson.
A good question would relate to the science content (e.g., 'Why does the moon change shape?').
solution.answer: B) No — the question is not connected to the speaker's topic.

items.prompt: A speaker says: 'Honeybees are very important to farmers because they pollinate crops. Without bees, many of our fruits and vegetables might not grow.' A student asks: 'What does pollinate mean?' Is this a good question?

steps: Yes — the student identified a word she did not understand from the speaker's statement.
Asking for clarification of vocabulary is a good question about what the speaker said.
This directly relates to a key term the speaker used.
solution.answer: Yes — asking about an unclear word ('pollinate') directly from the speaker's statement is an excellent clarifying question.

items.prompt: A speaker says: 'Last summer I hiked up a mountain for the first time. I was nervous, but my dad helped me every step of the way.' A student wants to ask a question to get more information. What should she ask?

steps: To get MORE information, the question should open up a new detail the speaker has not yet shared.
Good questions: 'How tall was the mountain?' or 'How did your dad help you?' or 'Were you scared at the top?'
These questions invite the speaker to share more about her experience.
solution.answer: 'How did your dad help you?' or 'How long did the hike take?' — these questions gather additional information about the speaker's experience.

items.prompt:
A classmate says: 'I have a pet turtle named Shell. She likes to eat lettuce and sit under her warm lamp.' What question can you ask to get MORE information?
A) 'Do you like turtles?'
B) 'How long have you had Shell?'
items.hint: A good question for more information asks about something the speaker has not yet told you.

steps: Option A asks for the listener's opinion — not a question about the speaker's topic.
Option B asks about a detail not yet mentioned (how long she has had the turtle) — this gets more information from the speaker.
solution.answer: B) 'How long have you had Shell?' — this gathers new information about what the speaker said.

items.prompt: A teacher says: 'Today we will learn about habitats. A habitat is the natural home of an animal.' A student did not catch the definition. What question should she ask?
items.hint: Ask the speaker to repeat or explain the part that was confusing.

steps: She should ask the teacher to clarify the definition.
Good question: 'Can you explain what a habitat is again?' or 'What did you say a habitat was?'
solution.answer: 'Can you explain what a habitat is?' — this asks the speaker to clarify the part the student missed.

items.prompt:
A student presents about her trip to the beach. She says: 'We found shells and built a big sandcastle.' A classmate asks: 'How big was the sandcastle?' Is this a good question?
A) Yes — it asks for more detail about what the speaker said.
B) No — it is rude.
items.hint: Think about whether the question connects to the speaker's topic.

steps: Yes — the speaker mentioned a 'big sandcastle.' Asking how big it was connects directly to that detail.
This is a good question for gathering additional information.
solution.answer: A) Yes — it asks for more detail about something the speaker mentioned.

items.prompt:
A visitor comes to class and talks about being a firefighter. He mentions they use special equipment. A student asks: 'What special equipment do you use?' Is this a good question?
A) Yes
B) No
items.hint: Is the question connected to what the speaker said?

steps: The speaker mentioned 'special equipment' but did not name it.
Asking 'what special equipment' directly follows up on something the speaker said.
This is an excellent question for gathering more information.
solution.answer: A) Yes — the question follows up on a detail the speaker mentioned.

items.prompt: A teacher gives a short talk about caterpillars turning into butterflies. After the talk, a student asks: 'How long does it take a caterpillar to become a butterfly?' The teacher said the chrysalis stage takes about 2 weeks. How should the student answer if someone asks: 'What did the teacher say about timing?'
items.hint: Recall what the speaker specifically said.

steps: The teacher said the chrysalis stage takes about 2 weeks.
A complete answer: 'The teacher said the chrysalis stage takes about two weeks.'
solution.answer: The teacher said it takes about 2 weeks for a caterpillar to become a butterfly (in the chrysalis stage).
